<hypothesis>
The first experiment showed that all mechanisms fit nearly identically, indicating that the moderate baseline conditions do not create sufficient mechanistic divergence. This is expected because many mechanisms can produce similar overall kinetic profiles under non-extreme conditions.

To discriminate among mechanisms, I need to exploit their **fundamental structural differences**:

1. **Catalyst concentration effects**: 
   - M1, M4: Simple Michaelis-Menten (rate ∝ [cat])
   - M2, M3, M13: Catalyst dimerization (rate ∝ [cat] or [cat]^2 depending on regime)
   - M6, M8: Catalyst activation/ligand dissociation (rate may show non-linear [cat] dependence)
   - M9-M20: Deactivation mechanisms (rate should decay over time)

2. **Strategy**: Use **very low catalyst concentration** (5×10^-4) to:
   - Amplify the effect of catalyst-dependent kinetics
   - Make dimerization effects more pronounced (if present)
   - Reveal whether activation/deactivation pathways are rate-limiting
   - Create conditions where different mechanisms predict divergent behaviors

3. **Why this works**: At low [cat], mechanisms with catalyst dimerization (M2, M3, M13) will show dramatically reduced rates compared to simple Michaelis-Menten (M1), because the equilibrium 2cat ⇌ cat2 shifts toward monomers. Conversely, mechanisms with catalyst activation (M6, M8) may show different concentration dependencies. Deactivation mechanisms (M9-M20) will show time-dependent rate decay.

This experiment will create **mechanistic divergence** by pushing the system into a regime where different mechanisms make qualitatively different predictions.
</hypothesis>
